title: Remember: Accept the Stalemate
summary: Recognize a protected checking rook that can be sacrificed for stalemate, and distinguish that draw from a repeated-check defense.

nodes.question: Can Black avoid the draw after Rb7+?
nodes.explanation: Black has only Bxb7 or Ka6. Capturing the rook with the bishop stalemates White; declining lets White repeat protected checks on a7 and b7. Independent non-loss strategies for both sides establish the exact draw.

branches.title: Take the rook and confirm the stalemate
commentary: Begin after Rb7+. The white king on b8 protects the checking rook, so Kxb7 is illegal. Ka6 is the only legal king escape; White can answer Ra7+ and repeat checks if Black declines the sacrifice.

Bxb7 removes White’s only mobile rook. Kb6 and Bb7 cover the white king’s escape squares without checking Kb8; b4 is blocked by b5, and d3 by d4. White has no legal move and is not in check: actual stalemate, despite Black’s promoted queen, rook and pawns.

exercises.prompt: Why can the king not capture the checking rook?
exercises.answer: White Kb8 protects b7. Black can either capture with Bc6 or move the king to a6.

exercises.prompt: Why does declining the sacrifice still fail to win?
exercises.answer: Ka6 allows Ra7+. Kb6 is then forced, and Rb7+ restores the checked position. The saved proof follows legal history until White can claim threefold repetition; Black may also choose Bxb7 and immediate stalemate.
